newsitem.title: USA: U.S. health panel updates asthma guidelines.
newsitem.headline: U.S. health panel updates asthma guidelines.

text.p: Health experts released revised guidelines Monday for the diagnosis and treatment of asthma, a disease that afflicts 14 million to 15 million people in the United States and kills more than 5,000 each year.

The report, released by the National Asthma Education and Prevention Programme, said it was essential to reduce the exposure of patients to allergens and that asthma onset could be prevented by reducing exposure to tobacco smoke.

The report, based on a review of asthma studies over the past six years, recommended a new approach to using asthma medications that would put greater emphasis on early use of anti-inflammatory drugs. It also stressed the importance of treating young children, who it said had been under-diagnosed and under-treated.

"Asthma is still a major public health problem in the U.S.," said Shirley Murphy, head of the Department of Pediatrics at the University of New Mexico and of the expert panel that prepared the report. She said it was time for doctors to "take asthma seriously and treat it aggressively."

Asthma, a chronic inflammatory disease of the lung airways, is the most common chronic disease of childhood, affecting an estimated 4.8 million children. Asthma hospitalization rates are highest among blacks and children, while death rates are consistently highest among blacks age 15 to 24, the report said.
The cost of asthma care exceeds $4.6 billion a year, according to the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute.

The "Report of the Second Expert Panel on the Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Asthma," which updates the first asthma clinical practice guidelines released in 1991, was presented at an American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology meeting in San Francisco.
It was prepared by a 22-member panel and was approved by the National Asthma Education and Prevention Program's coordinating committee. The report will be converted into a guide for doctors.
The new report does not represent a major departure from the first guidelines but rather "an evolution," Murphy said.

"It strengthens all the themes of the first report, including the critical role of inflammation in asthma and the importance of a physician/patient partnership in managing the disease," she said. "But the new report also reflects our improved understanding of how to diagnose and manage this serious condition and adds important recommendations that should help clinicians and patients make appropriate decisions about asthma care."

For successful asthma management, Murphy said it was essential to identify and reduce patient exposure to allergens and irritants as well as to control other factors that have been shown to increase asthma symptoms.

Persistent asthma must be controlled with daily anti-inflammatory medications, Murphy said, adding that the panel strongly recommended that physicians measure lung function and asthma patients monitor their disease at home.
